      Toner: Improving Muon and AdamW with Input Geometry

      Mohamad Amin MohamadiTTIC
      Kaiyue WenStanford
      Tianhao WangUCSD
      Zhiyuan LiTTIC

      TL;DR

      • We introduce Toner11Named after skincare toners: a lightweight conditioning for uneven features., a general preconditioning rule that uses each layer’s input statistics. Applied to Muon and AdamW as MuonT and AdamT, it lowers validation loss in language-model pretraining, especially at larger batch sizes.
      • We find that the inputs to transformer layers are strongly anisotropic: activations have much larger components along some directions than others. This observation motivated the development of Toner.
      • Our experiments show improvements over Muon across 130M–1.2B models, multiple batch sizes, and 1×–8× Chinchilla training budgets for the 130M model. On 1.2B models, Toner achieves estimated token savings of up to 22% at the same loss while adding only about 1.5% to total training time. Our results also suggest that MuonT can roughly double Muon’s critical batch size in some of the settings we study.

      In this post

      Section 1 introduces Muon and how it changes a layer’s outputs (its features), Section 2 examines how the inputs affect those changes, Section 3 develops Toner from these observations, Section 4 evaluates its training performance, and Section 5 investigates what contributes to the gains.

      Code & reproduction configs on GitHub

      1Background: Muon

      Muon has helped set NanoGPT and CIFAR-10 speedrun records [1][1]K. Jordan et al. Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks, 2024., ranked among the fastest optimizers in Marin's benchmark [2][2]K. Wen et al. Fantastic pretraining optimizers and where to find them, 2025., and been shown to scale to trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models [3, 4][3]J. Liu et al. Muon is scalable for LLM training, 2025.[4]Kimi Team. Kimi K3: Open frontier intelligence, 2026..

      Muon constructs an update for each hidden weight matrix by orthogonalizing its momentum matrix MMM. Writing the thin singular value decomposition as M=UΣV⊤M=U\Sigma V^{\top}M=UΣV⊤, the ideal direction is polar⁡(M)=UV⊤\polar(M)=UV^{\top}polar(M)=UV⊤, the polar factor of MMM. Muon approximates it with a short Newton–Schulz iteration.

      To understand what this normalization means for a layer's outputs (its features), consider a linear layer y=Wxy=Wxy=Wx. For a fixed input xxx, a weight update ΔW\Delta WΔW changes the layer's output by Δy=ΔWx\Delta y=\Delta WxΔy=ΔWx. The effect of the update therefore depends not only on the update matrix itself, but also on the inputs to which it is applied. When the momentum matrix MMM has full column rank, Muon's exact polar direction preserves the length of every input vector. In particular, under ΔW=polar⁡(M)\Delta W=\polar(M)ΔW=polar(M), every input with ∥x∥2=1\|x\|_2=1∥x∥2​=1 produces an output change with ∥Δy∥2=1\|\Delta y\|_2=1∥Δy∥2​=1.22These statements concern the exact polar direction before learning-rate scaling and weight decay. Wide matrices introduce a projection factor, and finite Newton–Schulz updates need not have equal directional lengths. Appendix A1 gives the algebraic conditions.

      Training inputs need not have equally large components in every direction, so equal responses to unit inputs can still produce uneven feature changes. This raises a natural question: can we improve Muon by accounting for the distribution of inputs when constructing its updates? To investigate, we measure how layer inputs vary across directions in transformer language models and calculate the feature changes implied by Muon's ideal update. These observations motivate Toner.

      2Input Anisotropy and Feature Changes

      2.1Measuring Input Energy

      We examined the inputs to the 32 attention layers of a Muon-trained Marin 130M model, a Llama-style decoder-only transformer. Treating the layer’s input xxx as random over its input distribution, we define the input energy along a fixed unit direction vvv as E[(v⊤x)2]\E[(v^{\top}x)^2]E[(v⊤x)2]. This lets us compare directions and quantify how concentrated the input energy is.

      To find the directions with the most energy, we use the input second-moment matrix C=E[xx⊤]C=\E[xx^{\top}]C=E[xx⊤]. Its unit eigenvectors {vi}i=1n\{v_i\}_{i=1}^{n}{vi​}i=1n​ are orthogonal input directions, and each eigenvalue is the energy along one of them: λi=E[(vi⊤x)2]\lambda_i=\E[(v_i^{\top}x)^2]λi​=E[(vi⊤​x)2]. We therefore study the spectrum of CCC.

      Across these layers, the largest eigenvalue is 85–156 times the mean eigenvalue in its layer, while about 80% of directions have below-mean energy (Figure 2). We observe a similar pattern in our nanoGPT setup.33We average over sampled token positions without centering the inputs. The Marin measurement uses the final checkpoint after 2.7B training tokens at a 1M-token batch. On the nanoGPT model, the top eigenvalue is a median 129 times the mean across hidden-matrix inputs, with a range of about 20–1,850. Du and Su also report strongly anisotropic input second moments in their Newton–Muon experiments [5].

      2.2From Inputs to Feature Changes

      To connect these spectra to feature changes, we combine input energy with the update's response along each input direction. For a weight update ΔW\Delta WΔW, excluding weight decay, the input projection (vi⊤x)vi(v_i^{\top}x)v_i(vi⊤​x)vi​ produces the output change (vi⊤x)ΔWvi(v_i^{\top}x)\Delta Wv_i(vi⊤​x)ΔWvi​. Its root mean square (RMS) length is

      E∥(vi⊤x) ΔWvi∥22=λi ∥ΔWvi∥2.\sqrt{\E\|(v_i^{\top}x)\,\Delta Wv_i\|_2^2}=\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,\|\Delta Wv_i\|_2.E∥(vi⊤​x)ΔWvi​∥22​​=λi​​∥ΔWvi​∥2​.

      The first factor is the RMS input size in that direction; the second is the response to a unit input. Because the {vi}i=1n\{v_i\}_{i=1}^{n}{vi​}i=1n​ diagonalize CCC, cross terms vanish after averaging, and the squared lengths sum to the total mean squared feature change:

      E∥ΔWx∥22=∑iλi∥ΔWvi∥22.\E\|\Delta Wx\|_2^2=\sum_i\lambda_i\|\Delta Wv_i\|_2^2.E∥ΔWx∥22​=i∑​λi​∥ΔWvi​∥22​.

      For the ideal Muon update, ∥ΔWvi∥2=1\|\Delta Wv_i\|_2=1∥ΔWvi​∥2​=1 for every direction, so each direction's share of the mean squared feature change is its share of input energy, λi/tr⁡C\lambda_i/\tr Cλi​/trC. In the Marin spectra (Figure 2), the single leading direction takes a median 21%.

      This concentration need not be harmful, but it motivated us to try updates that respond less strongly to high-energy input directions relative to low-energy ones.

      3Toner: Preconditioning with Input Statistics

      3.1Constructing the Update

      To incorporate the input distribution, we construct the optimizer’s update in coordinates where input energy is more evenly distributed, then map the step back. This idea applies to different base optimizers; we first work through Muon.

      To do so, we use a transformation R∝C−α\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}\propto C^{-\alpha}R∝C−α with strength α>0\alpha>0α>0, where C=E[xx⊤]C=\E[xx^{\top}]C=E[xx⊤] is the input second-moment matrix from Section 2.1. This transformation reduces high-energy input components relative to low-energy ones. Writing

      x~=Rx,W=W~R\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde x}=\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}x,\qquad W=\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde W} \htmlClass{k-toner}{R}x~=Rx,W=W~R

      expresses the same linear layer as

      y=Wx=W~x~.y=Wx=\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde W}\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde x}.y=Wx=W~x~.

      To apply Muon in these coordinates, we first transform the momentum. With R\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}R held fixed, the gradient GGG with respect to WWW becomes GRG\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}GR, and the corresponding momentum becomes MRM\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}MR. Muon's polar operation then gives the update direction polar⁡(MR)\polar(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{R})polar(MR) for W~\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde W}W~. Since W=W~RW=\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde W} \htmlClass{k-toner}{R}W=W~R, we multiply this direction by R\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}R to obtain the update in the original weight coordinates:

      D=polar⁡(MR)R.D=\polar(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{R})\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}.D=polar(MR)R.

      We call the factor inside the polar operation the inner factor, and the one afterward the outer factor.

      We take inspiration from K-FAC’s use of the input second moment [6][6]J. Martens and R. Grosse. Optimizing neural networks with Kronecker-factored approximate curvature, 2015.. We can interpret the matched-factor update as steepest feature descent, where the step-size constraint accounts for the layer’s inputs. Section 5.1 explains this interpretation, and Appendix A1 gives the derivation.44GO-MUON [7] and Newton–Muon [5] have similar update forms. Section 3.4 compares their updates with Toner’s.

      The inner factor reweights the momentum before Muon’s polar operation. The outer factor maps the resulting update back to the original weight coordinates.

      3.2Decoupling the Inner and Outer Strengths

      The coordinate construction uses the same transformation for both factors, but they affect the update differently. In the ideal full-column-rank case, the inner factor changes the orientations of the update’s responses to input directions, while the outer factor sets their lengths. We suspected that gradient noise could affect their useful strengths differently: orientation changes might remain helpful at smaller batch sizes even when strong rescaling gives too much weight to noisy directions. We therefore tested separate inner and outer strengths, denoted by aaa and bbb:55 Figure 13 reports curvature and directional-noise probes from the earlier (¼, ¼) study. These do not isolate the noise sensitivity of the two factors.

      D=polar⁡(MRa) Rb,Ra∝C−a,Rb∝C−b.D=\polar(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_a})\,\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b},\qquad \htmlClass{k-toner}{R_a}\propto C^{-a},\quad \htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b}\propto C^{-b}.D=polar(MRa​)Rb​,Ra​∝C−a,Rb​∝C−b.

      We compare inner and outer strengths across batch sizes and learning rates in nanoGPT (Figure 3). The results support (½, ⅛) as a robust choice across the tested settings. At the baseline Muon learning rate (the 1× setting in Figure 3), (¾, ⅛) achieves slightly lower loss at batch sizes of 1M and 2M tokens. We use (½, ⅛) as a fixed configuration across our main experiments and recommend it as a robust default for practical use.66Appendix A3 describes the training setups and tuning procedure.

      3.3Toner in Practice

      During training, we estimate CCC from sampled layer inputs. Before taking inverse powers, we damp the statistic to limit amplification of very low-energy directions. We then normalize each factor to keep its overall scale fixed. With nnn input coordinates, the update is

      A=n Ctr⁡C+ϵI,Rq=n A−q∥A−q∥F,DMuonT=polar⁡(MRa)Rb,ΔW=−η(sDMuonT+λWRb2).\begin{aligned} \htmlClass{k-toner}{A} &= \htmlClass{k-toner}{\frac{n\,C}{\tr C}+\epsilon I},\\ \htmlClass{k-toner}{R_q} &= \htmlClass{k-toner}{\frac{\sqrt n\,A^{-q}}{\|A^{-q}\|_F}},\\ \htmlClass{k-toner}{D_{\mathrm{MuonT}}} &= \htmlClass{k-muon}{\polar}(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_a})\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b},\\ \Delta W &= -\eta\bigl(s\htmlClass{k-toner}{D_{\mathrm{MuonT}}}+\lambda W\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b^2}\bigr). \end{aligned}ARq​DMuonT​ΔW​=trCnC​+ϵI,=∥A−q∥F​n​A−q​,=polar(MRa​)Rb​,=−η(sDMuonT​+λWRb2​).​(1)

      Here η\etaη is the learning rate, λ\lambdaλ is the decay coefficient, and sss is Muon's matrix-shape scaling. Our recipe uses (a,b)=(12,18)(a,b)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac18)(a,b)=(21​,81​). An inner strength of ½ approximately standardizes input directions before the polar operation, while an outer strength of ⅛ makes a milder adjustment afterward. From here on, MuonT refers to this configuration unless otherwise specified.

      Shaping the Weight Decay

      Toner changes the relative sizes of updates along input directions, so we also examined how these updates interact with weight decay. Plain decay shrinks weights by the same fraction in every direction. After observing that it could erase Toner’s gain, we tested decay shaped by the same input statistics.77Direction-dependent shrinkage also arises from preconditioned L2L_2L2​ regularization; see Equation 6 in Zhang et al. [8]. We use WRb2W\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b^2}WRb2​, giving relatively weaker shrinkage along high-energy directions and stronger shrinkage along low-energy ones.88For fixed R\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}R, a separate gradient step on the original-weight penalty λ∥W∥F2/2\lambda\|W\|_F^2/2λ∥W∥F2​/2, expressed in coordinates W=W~RW=\htmlClass{k-toner}{\tilde W} \htmlClass{k-toner}{R}W=W~R and mapped back, gives −ηλWR2-\eta\lambda W\htmlClass{k-toner}{R^2}−ηλWR2. We retain this form with R=Rb\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}=\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b}R=Rb​ when separating the update strengths. Appendix A1 gives the derivation.

      With the MuonT update fixed, shaped decay gives lower validation loss than plain decay at all four tested batch sizes, using the same scalar decay coefficient (Figure 7).

      Toner acts on the hidden weight matrices; embeddings, the output head and normalization parameters keep their baseline updates. Earlier learning-rate comparisons led us to multiply the base Muon configuration's hidden-matrix learning rate by 2\sqrt22​. In the main Marin comparisons, we keep this multiplier and the strengths fixed, inheriting the base configuration's decay coefficient and remaining settings.99Figure 12 lists the recorded hyperparameters under “Run settings.” Section 5.3 reports the follow-up learning-rate sweep.

      3.4Relation to Other Optimizers

      Toner uses input statistics to precondition an optimizer’s update. Several existing methods use similar statistics, so it is useful to distinguish how they enter the update. Block-diagonal K-FAC [6], for example, approximates layerwise curvature using two factors: the input second moment CCC and an output-gradient factor B=E[δδ⊤]B=\E[\delta\delta^{\top}]B=E[δδ⊤], where δ\deltaδ is the loss gradient with respect to the layer’s output and the expectation is over training inputs, with targets sampled from the model. MuonT uses only the input statistic CCC.

      The following update formulas show how K-FAC, Newton–Muon and MuonT use these factors differently, omitting momentum, damping, decay and overall scaling:

      MethodSchematic update
      K-FAC−ηB−1GC−1-\eta B^{-1}GC^{-1}−ηB−1GC−1
      Newton–Muon−η polar⁡(GC−1)-\eta\,\polar(GC^{-1})−ηpolar(GC−1)
      MuonT−η polar⁡(GRa)Rb-\eta\,\polar(G\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_a})\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b}−ηpolar(GRa​)Rb​

      Like MuonT, Newton–Muon combines input preconditioning with Muon’s polar operation [5][5]Z. Du and W. Su. The Newton–Muon optimizer, 2026.. It applies C−1C^{-1}C−1 before the polar operation, but has no outer factor. It also preconditions gradients before accumulating momentum, whereas MuonT applies the current inner factor to the accumulated momentum. This ordering matters when the input statistics change during training.

      GO-MUON [7][7]T. Che. Second-order Muon done right: A principled marriage of spectral geometry and curvature (GO-MUON), 2026. applies preconditioning both before and after the polar operation, using input and output statistics. If we keep only its input factors, we recover polar⁡(MR)R\polar(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{R})\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}polar(MR)R, the matched-factor update we started with in Section 3.1. MuonT separates the strengths of these two factors and uses the outer factor to shape weight decay through WRb2W\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b^2}WRb2​.

      Beyond these update formulas, the methods differ in how they estimate input statistics, refresh the factors and approximate the polar operation. Our adapted Newton–Muon comparisons show that these choices affect training loss; Appendix A6 describes the comparisons and implementation differences.

      Earlier activation-aware Muon experiments with Ali Jadbabaie. Ali Jadbabaie previously proposed an activation-aware Muon update, polar⁡(MC−1/2)C−1/2\polar(MC^{-1/2})C^{-1/2}polar(MC−1/2)C−1/2, which Kaiyue Wen implemented and tested in Marin. Up to scalar normalization, this update is the special case of Toner’s preconditioning rule with inner and outer strengths (½, ½). Toner allows these strengths to differ and introduces shaped weight decay, whereas the earlier implementation used ordinary weight decay. Our ablations show that these choices are important for the gains we observe (Figures 7 and 8).

      4Results

      4.1Setup and Evaluation

      We evaluate MuonT on Marin's Llama-style models [9, 2][9]The Marin community. Marin: an open lab for building foundation models.: the 130M, 300M, 520M and 1.2B models. Our main metric, C4 loss, is the final cross-entropy loss on held-out C4 text from the Paloma suite [10][10]I. Magnusson et al. Paloma: A benchmark for evaluating language model fit, 2023.. At each model size, the batch-size comparisons use the same architecture, training data and token budget—about 20 tokens per parameter [11][11]J. Hoffmann et al. Training compute-optimal large language models, 2022., counting non-embedding parameters.1111The model-size labels exclude token embeddings and the output head. Batch size means tokens per optimizer update; 1M in batch labels denotes 2202^{20}220 tokens. Appendix A3 gives the setups.

      The GitHub repository includes the hyperparameters and reproduction instructions for our main Marin and nanoGPT experiments.

      We start from Marin's tuned Muon settings. For the 130M–520M models, we use Dang et al.'s transfer rules [12][12]X. Dang et al. The best optimizer depends on batch size, 2026. to choose initial settings at larger batch sizes, then refine the baseline by varying one hyperparameter at a time. The 1.2B model comparison uses transferred settings with a smaller baseline search.1212For the 1.2B model, batch 1M uses Marin's tuned reference; 2M and 8M use transferred settings without a search; 4M uses the lower-loss of two learning rates. Appendix A3 gives the comparison settings.

      For the scaling and longer-training comparisons, we emphasize that MuonT applies a fixed rule to the base Muon configurations, using the same strengths and learning-rate multiplier from Section 3.3 across these comparisons. We do not run a separate MuonT hyperparameter search at each setting, so additional tuning could yield further gains.

      To express a loss difference in training tokens, we estimate how much training the baseline would need to reach Toner's final loss. At the same batch size, if Toner uses SToner\htmlClass{k-toner}{S_{\mathrm{Toner}}}SToner​ updates to reach LToner\htmlClass{k-toner}{L_{\mathrm{Toner}}}LToner​, its estimated saving is

      saving=1−SToner / Sbase(LToner),\text{saving} = 1 - \htmlClass{k-toner}{S_{\mathrm{Toner}}} \,/\, S_{\mathrm{base}}(\htmlClass{k-toner}{L_{\mathrm{Toner}}}),saving=1−SToner​/Sbase​(LToner​),(2)

      where Sbase(L)S_{\mathrm{base}}(L)Sbase​(L) is the number of updates the baseline needs to reach loss LLL. We estimate it with power-law fits to final losses at different training budgets, each with a completed learning-rate schedule. At a fixed batch size, saving a fraction of the updates saves the same fraction of tokens. Appendix A2 describes the fitting assumptions and sensitivity checks.

      4.2Scaling Across Model and Batch Sizes

      MuonT lowers C4 loss across 130M–1.2B models, with larger gains at larger batch sizes (Figure 1). This batch-size trend is consistent with Zhang et al.'s analysis [13][13]G. Zhang et al. Which algorithmic choices matter at which batch sizes? Insights from a noisy quadratic model. NeurIPS, 2019.: the benefits of preconditioning can become more pronounced as larger batch sizes reduce gradient noise.

      At the smallest tested batch sizes, the two methods reach similar losses. At a 4M-token batch, the estimated token savings range from 13–24% across the four model sizes. For the 1.2B model, the estimate is about 22% at 8M. These savings measure the improvement over Muon at the same batch size.

      The larger gains at large batch sizes suggest that Toner mitigates some of the optimization cost of large-batch training. The savings at a fixed batch size should therefore not be read as a model-size trend. Figure 10 explores how batch size and training length affect the gains in our earlier (¼, ¼) experiments on the 130M model.1313Appendix A2 explains the critical-batch estimates used in the figure.

      AdamT, using the (¼, ¼) factors introduced in Section 3.3, also lowers C4 loss relative to tuned AdamW in the Marin comparisons (Figure 1, AdamW view). At a 2M-token batch, the estimated token savings are about 24% for the 130M model and 15% for the 300M model.1414We tune AdamW using the same batch-transfer and coordinate-search procedure.

      We also use the modded-nanoGPT setup of Dang et al. [12], training a 162M model on FineWeb and comparing against their published baselines, tuned separately at each batch size.1515This nanoGPT setup is sensitive to data shuffling [14]: shuffled training rows lower final validation loss by about 0.01–0.02 nats for every optimizer tested, so we keep the original unshuffled loader for consistency. MuonT’s advantage over Muon again grows with batch size (Figure 11 in Appendix A4). We keep MuonT’s strengths fixed and select a learning rate at each batch from the grids in Section 3.2.

      4.3Training Longer

      MuonT retains a loss advantage when we train the Marin 130M model for up to eight times its base budget of 2.7B tokens, reaching 21.5B tokens. The critical batch size is the point beyond which increasing the batch size stops reducing the number of updates needed. Prior work observes that it grows approximately with the square root of the number of training tokens [15, 16][15]H. Zhang et al. How does critical batch size scale in pre-training?, 2024.[16]S. Bergsma et al. Power lines: Scaling laws for weight decay and batch size in LLM pre-training, 2025.. We follow this scaling when increasing the training budget, using a 1M-token batch at the 1× budget and increasing it to about 2.8M tokens at 8×.1616 In the earlier (¼, ¼) study, holding batch size fixed instead reduces the estimated advantage with longer training. Appendix A2 compares the two schedules. We re-tune Muon at each budget and keep MuonT’s strengths and 2\sqrt22​ learning-rate multiplier fixed.

      Under power-law loss scaling, a similar percentage saving in tokens corresponds to a smaller absolute loss gap at longer training budgets. Here, the loss gap narrows from about 0.024 to 0.012 nats while estimated token savings remain around 10–13% (Figure 4).

      4.4Larger Batch Sizes and Fewer Updates

      The fixed-token loss-versus-batch curves in Figure 1 suggest that MuonT can roughly double Muon’s critical batch size in some of the settings we study. For example, the 1.2B model reaches a final C4 loss of 2.8936 with MuonT at a 4M-token batch, compared with 2.8986 for Muon at a 2M-token batch, using the same training budget.

      With enough parallel hardware, a larger batch can process the same tokens in fewer sequential updates and shorten training, provided it does not require more tokens to reach the target loss [17][17]S. McCandlish et al. An empirical model of large-batch training, 2018.. We thus test whether MuonT can use a larger batch while keeping the token budget and final loss comparable.

      For this comparison, we train the Marin 130M model with both optimizers on the same 2.7B tokens, using a 0.5M-token batch for Muon and a 0.75M-token batch for MuonT. The larger batch uses one third fewer updates—3,413 instead of 5,120—while reaching a slightly lower final C4 loss: 3.4571 versus 3.4621.

      Critical batch size can grow rapidly early in training [18][18]W. Merrill et al. Critical batch size revisited: A simple empirical approach to large-batch language model training. NeurIPS, 2025., motivating a smaller initial batch followed by an increase. We therefore repeat the comparison with batch sizes that gradually increase during this phase. MuonT again uses two-thirds as many updates, with final loss about 0.0016 nats lower (Figure 5).1717 Seesaw [19] also studies increasing batch size during training, jointly with learning-rate scheduling. The caption of Figure 5 gives our batch schedules; Appendix A7 discusses computational overhead.

      5Analysis

      5.1Orientation and Rescaling

      Our original motivation was to make feature changes more even. Applying the ideal update formulas to the same measured Marin attention-input spectra, the single leading direction’s median share of the mean squared feature change is 21% under Muon, 7.9% under MuonT with (a,b)=(12,18)(a,b)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac18)(a,b)=(21​,81​), and 2.5% with matched (14,14)(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)(41​,41​) factors. Yet MuonT with (12,18)(\tfrac12,\tfrac18)(21​,81​) factors trains better in several comparisons. This measure of evenness therefore does not, by itself, predict which recipe trains best.

      Changing Orientations and Lengths Separately

      The feature-energy shares do not capture output orientations. To test their effect, we continue from a shared nanoGPT checkpoint. For an input eigenvector viv_ivi​, the update’s response is the output change DviDv_iDvi​. We replace selected Muon responses with those from the inner-only (14,0)(\tfrac14,0)(41​,0) update, keeping their lengths approximately unchanged. Changing only responses to high-energy inputs improves final loss by 0.0037 nats, close to the 0.0042 improvement from changing the responses in all square and tall matrices. Changing only low-energy responses gives a 0.0006 improvement (Figure 6, left).1818The replacements approximately preserve each input eigenvector's response length. Combining them need not preserve mutual orthogonality or lengths for arbitrary inputs. Wide matrices keep Muon's update; Appendix A8 describes the intervention.

      Shuffling the directional weights or using a random input basis removes most of the gain. The measured input directions matter here, although these controls also change how much the responses rotate.

      In separate runs trained from scratch, we test what outer scaling adds while keeping the inner strength at ½, learning rate and shaped decay fixed. Moving from (12,0)(\tfrac12,0)(21​,0) to (12,14)(\tfrac12,\tfrac14)(21​,41​) lowers final loss by 0.0100 nats (Figure 6, right). Outer scaling therefore helps even when the decay rule stays unchanged.

      Geometry and the steepest-descent interpretation

      Measuring a Step Through the Layer’s Inputs

      Steepest descent depends on how we measure the size of a step. Muon’s ideal polar update has a steepest-descent interpretation under a spectral-norm constraint [20][20]J. Bernstein and L. Newhouse. Old optimizer, new norm: An anthology, 2024.. The norm ∥ΔW∥op\|\Delta W\|_{\op}∥ΔW∥op​ measures the largest output change caused by a unit input. This treats all unit input directions alike, although the layer’s actual inputs can have very different magnitudes along them.

      To account for those inputs, consider the feature change ΔWx\Delta W xΔWx. Along a unit output direction uuu, this change is u⊤ΔWxu^{\top}\Delta W xu⊤ΔWx. We measure its RMS over the input distribution, then take the largest value across output directions:

      max⁡∥u∥2=1E[(u⊤ΔWx)2]=∥ΔWC1/2∥op.\max_{\|u\|_2=1}\sqrt{\E[(u^{\top}\Delta W x)^2]} =\|\Delta W C^{1/2}\|_{\op}.∥u∥2​=1max​E[(u⊤ΔWx)2]​=∥ΔWC1/2∥op​.(3)
      max⁡∥u∥2=1E[(u⊤ΔWx)2]=∥ΔWC1/2∥op.\begin{aligned}&\max_{\|u\|_2=1}\sqrt{\E[(u^{\top}\Delta W x)^2]}\\ &\quad=\|\Delta W C^{1/2}\|_{\op}.\end{aligned}​∥u∥2​=1max​E[(u⊤ΔWx)2]​=∥ΔWC1/2∥op​.​(3)

      Under this measure, a weight change along a high-energy input direction uses more of the allowed feature change. The input distribution therefore changes which weight updates count as small.

      More generally, let a fixed symmetric positive-definite R\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}R define the constraint ∥ΔWR−1∥op≤η\|\Delta W \htmlClass{k-toner}{R^{-1}}\|_{\op}\le\eta∥ΔWR−1∥op​≤η. In the coordinates from Section 3, this becomes Muon’s usual spectral-norm constraint. The gradient becomes GRG\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}GR; taking the polar step there and mapping it back gives

      ΔW⋆=−η polar⁡(GR)R.\Delta W^\star=-\eta\,\polar(G\htmlClass{k-toner}{R})\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}.ΔW⋆=−ηpolar(GR)R.(4)

      Both factors arise from the same coordinate transformation, so this construction ties their strengths. For positive-definite CCC, taking R=C−1/2\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}=C^{-1/2}R=C−1/2 gives the feature-RMS constraint above; taking R=C−1/4\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}=C^{-1/4}R=C−1/4 instead constrains ∥ΔWC1/4∥op\|\Delta W C^{1/4}\|_{\op}∥ΔWC1/4∥op​, giving input energy a weaker influence.

      What the Energy Shares Leave Out

      We can also make the distinction between orientations and lengths precise. Write D=ORbD=O\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b}D=ORb​, where O=polar⁡(MRa)O=\polar(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_a})O=polar(MRa​). When the momentum has full column rank, the exact polar factor preserves lengths. Changing the inner factor can turn the response to an input direction without changing its length.

      The outer factor then sets that length. Without damping, its scaling along viv_ivi​ is proportional to λi−b\lambda_i^{-b}λi−b​. Combining this with the input energy λi\lambda_iλi​, the direction’s share of the mean squared feature change is

      λi∥Dvi∥22∑jλj∥Dvj∥22=λi1−2b∑jλj1−2b.\frac{\lambda_i\|Dv_i\|_2^2}{\sum_j\lambda_j\|Dv_j\|_2^2} =\frac{\lambda_i^{1-2b}}{\sum_j\lambda_j^{1-2b}}.∑j​λj​∥Dvj​∥22​λi​∥Dvi​∥22​​=∑j​λj1−2b​λi1−2b​​.(5)

      Only the outer strength appears. For example, (12,18)(\tfrac12,\tfrac18)(21​,81​) and (34,18)(\tfrac34,\tfrac18)(43​,81​) have the same ideal energy shares, even though their response orientations can differ. The energy calculation therefore leaves out the effect examined by the orientation experiments.

      The matched construction links these two operations through one step constraint. MuonT’s (12,18)(\tfrac12,\tfrac18)(21​,81​) recipe allows their strengths to differ, following the empirical findings; it does not generally solve the matched steepest-descent problem above.

      The steepest-descent derivation uses the gradient GGG; the implementation uses momentum. Appendix A1 gives the derivation and the wide-matrix case.

      5.2Input Energy, Curvature, and Noise

      Changing output orientations and rescaling response lengths both improve training in the preceding experiments. To relate these changes to the loss, our earlier (¼, ¼) studies measured curvature along input directions. At the examined checkpoints, the loss curvature along weight changes uvi⊤uv_i^{\top}uvi⊤​ grows roughly in proportion to the input energy λi\lambda_iλi​ (Figure 13). In these probes, high-energy inputs correspond to greater loss sensitivity, supporting smaller responses along those directions.

      Since MuonT’s advantage grows with batch size, we also study whether it depends on which input directions carry gradient noise. In our earlier (¼, ¼) study at a 2M-token batch, adding noise to gradient components associated with low-energy inputs reduces MuonT’s loss advantage over Muon by about 79%. Adding noise in high-energy directions increases its relative advantage. Both optimizers reach higher absolute losses under every added-noise condition (Figure 13, noise view). Where the noise is added matters, but these earlier studies do not yet explain MuonT’s batch-size dependence.

      5.3Weight Decay and Learning Rate

      Separating Outer Scaling from Weight Decay

      Our recipe uses the outer factor to shape both the update and weight decay. Changing its strength therefore changes two things at once, leaving unclear how much each contributes to the gain. We vary outer scaling and decay separately, with the inner strength fixed at ½, to distinguish their effects (Figure 7).

      With the MuonT update fixed, shaped decay gives lower loss than plain decay at all four tested batch sizes. With the decay strength fixed at ⅛, retaining outer scaling improves loss at three of the four batch sizes; omitting it is slightly better at 512K. Changing decay alone therefore does not account for all the benefit of the outer factor.

      Comparing Strengths Across Learning Rates

      A learning rate suited to one pair of strengths may put another at a disadvantage. After the scaling comparisons, we run a learning-rate sweep on the Marin 130M model to compare each strength pair at its best tested rate. MuonT still gives lower final loss than the (14,14)(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)(41​,41​) and (12,12)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(21​,21​) configurations at every tested batch size (Figure 8). Some batch sizes favor a rate different from the 2\sqrt22​ learning-rate multiplier from Section 3.3.

      Takeaway

      Using layer inputs to construct updates improves language-model training, especially at larger batch sizes. Our experiments suggest that making feature changes more even is only part of the story: changing update orientations also helps, and the inner and outer factors benefit from different strengths. We recommend MuonT with (½, ⅛) strengths and shaped weight decay as a robust practical default across the settings we tested. Our nanoGPT comparisons also suggest that (¾, ⅛) may give better results at larger batch sizes. Why MuonT’s advantage grows with batch size remains an open question.

      A2Estimating Training Efficiency

      We compare the tokens needed to reach the same final loss, using runs that complete their learning-rate schedules. We use the savings definition in (2).

      Token savings

      When we have baseline runs at several training budgets, we fit L=L∞+AN−pL=L_\infty+AN^{-p}L=L∞​+AN−p, where NNN is the token count. We fix L∞L_\inftyL∞​ from Marin’s reference curve at a 0.5M-token batch, then invert the fit to estimate the baseline step count in (2). For the 130M model, we have two or three budgets at each of the 1M, 2M and 4M batch sizes. At 0.5M, we use the reference curve directly.

      Estimates from one training budget

      With only one training budget, we instead transfer the batch-efficiency curve defined below using the growth exponent from the 130M studies. We assume that training for rrr times as many tokens at batch BBB has the base budget’s efficiency at B/r0.48B/r^{0.48}B/r0.48, keeping the curve’s shape fixed.

      AdamT. At batch 2M, the estimates for the 130M and 300M models use AdamW runs at two budgets. Elsewhere, we use AdamW losses with Muon’s budget exponent 0.372 and growth exponent 0.48. For the 520M model, we combine its AdamW loss at batch 1M with a fitted amplitude transferred from the 300M model.

      1.2B model. We fit the reference curve to Marin’s 1M-batch runs at 1×, 2× and 4× training. The 1M estimate uses this curve directly; the larger-batch estimates use the transfer assumption above.

      Sensitivity to fitting choices

      We check sensitivity by interpolating loss in log tokens. For MuonT on the 130M model at batch 4M, this gives 26.7% savings versus 24.2% from the power law; for the 1.2B model at batch 8M, it gives 26.4% versus 22.5%. AdamT’s estimate for the 130M model at batch 4M is more sensitive: the estimate of about 32% ranges from 26–41% under the tested scaling assumptions and extrapolates beyond the observed reference budgets. These ranges reflect fitting assumptions, not seed variability.

      Batch efficiency

      Larger batch sizes reduce the number of sequential updates, but can require more tokens to reach the same loss. Critical batch size describes where the reduction in updates stops keeping pace with the increase in batch size [17]. Preconditioning can raise this threshold [13]. Following Zhang et al. [15], we use a 20% token-overhead threshold for the earlier (¼, ¼) comparisons below.

      Batch size and training length together

      In our (¼, ¼) experiments on the 130M model, MuonT’s advantage over Muon depends on both batch size and training length. With a 1M-token batch, estimated token savings fall from about 9% to 3% as training extends from 1× to 4× the base budget. When we also increase the batch size, the savings remain more stable. Figure 10 places these results alongside the batch-size comparisons, where Toner helps more at larger batch sizes.

      Constructing the critical-batch guides

      To construct the dashed guides in Figure 10, let D0(L)D_0(L)D0​(L) be the reference-curve token count needed to reach loss LLL. At each training budget, we measure efficiency as D0(L)/D0(Lref)D_0(L)/D_0(L_{\mathrm{ref}})D0​(L)/D0​(Lref​), where LrefL_{\mathrm{ref}}Lref​ is the best 0.5M-batch Muon loss. We interpolate in log batch size to find where efficiency reaches 1/1.21/1.21/1.2.

      We fit power laws through the 1× and 4× thresholds and extrapolate to 8×, assuming equal efficiency at batch 0.5M where a Toner run is missing. The 2× and 8× studies each test one batch and cannot independently locate a threshold. Some savings estimates use the same growth assumption; their agreement with the guides is a consistency check.

      A5Update Rules

      To implement Algorithm 1, we estimate CCC from sampled layer inputs using an exponential moving average with coefficient 0.938.1919We fixed 0.938 during earlier explorations and retained it in these experiments. As a practical heuristic, we recommend matching the input-statistic momentum to Muon’s momentum coefficient. The primary Marin recipe uses the damped factors

      A=n Ctr⁡C+10−3I,R^q=A−q,Rq=n R^q/∥R^q∥F,(a,b)=(1/2,1/8).\begin{aligned} \htmlClass{k-toner}{A}&=\frac{n\,C}{\tr C}+10^{-3}I,\\ \htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R_q}&=\htmlClass{k-toner}{A^{-q}},\qquad \htmlClass{k-toner}{R_q}=\sqrt n\,\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R_q}/\|\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R_q}\|_F,\\ (a,b)&=(1/2,1/8). \end{aligned}AR^q​(a,b)​=trCnC​+10−3I,=A−q,Rq​=n​R^q​/∥R^q​∥F​,=(1/2,1/8).​

      We compute the factors separately and use WRb2W\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b^2}WRb2​ for decay. Appendix A3 describes scalar tuning; Figure 7 tests decay independently of outer scaling.

      We accumulate momentum in the original coordinates and evaluate NS(MR^a)Rb\mathrm{NS}(M\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R_a})\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_b}NS(MR^a​)Rb​. Muon’s shape factor s=max⁡(1,m/n)s=\sqrt{\max(1,m/n)}s=max(1,m/n)​ applies only to the adaptive update. Scalar normalization of the inner factor leaves the exact polar map unchanged, giving (1), though finite Newton–Schulz iterations can introduce numerical differences.

      AdamT's state and update

      AdamT (Algorithm 2) uses the original (¼, ¼) factors, R^=A−1/4\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R}=\htmlClass{k-toner}{A^{-1/4}}R^=A−1/4 and R=R1/4\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}=\htmlClass{k-toner}{R_{1/4}}R=R1/4​. We average the original gradient in the first moment and the entrywise squares of GR^G\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R}GR^ in the second. With bias-corrected moments m^\hat mm^ and v^\hat vv^, the update is

      U=m^R^/(v^+ϵAdam),ΔW=−η UR ∥U∥F∥UR∥F.U=\hat m\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R}/(\sqrt{\hat v}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{Adam}}),\qquad \Delta W=-\eta\,U\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}\,\frac{\|U\|_F}{\|U\htmlClass{k-toner}{R}\|_F}.U=m^R^/(v^​+ϵAdam​),ΔW=−ηUR∥UR∥F​∥U∥F​​.

      We take division and square root entrywise and preserve UUU’s norm when mapping back. This cancels a scalar rescaling of the outer factor. Rescaling the factor inside the accumulated second moment need not cancel, so we retain R^\htmlClass{k-toner}{\hat R}R^ there. Evolving factors make this state differ from Adam’s under a fixed change of coordinates. We use WR2W\htmlClass{k-toner}{R^2}WR2 for decay.

      A6Related Methods

      Section 3.4 compares the update formulas. Here we describe the implementation differences and our Newton–Muon comparisons.

      GO-MUON implementation

      GO-MUON uses OAS shrinkage for its input and output-gradient statistics, reuses factors between refreshes, and computes the polar factor by SVD [7]. MuonT uses a running input statistic, damping relative to its mean eigenvalue, and finite Newton–Schulz iterations. For matched factors, the normalization rules agree when the exact polar map has orthonormal columns; they need not agree for wide matrices. MuonT also includes shaped weight decay.

      Newton–Muon comparisons

      Our nanoGPT adaptations of Newton–Muon [5] improve on Muon but reach higher loss than the (¼, ¼) MuonT recipe. Updating the input statistics and factors every step, and using full matrices instead of MLP blocks, brings their losses closer to MuonT’s.

      These are adaptations of the published optimizer: we sample inputs, precondition after momentum, and use a different numerical polar approximation. The improvement reflects the combined changes to statistics, refresh and matrix structure.

      Broader connections

      Toner builds on the idea of using layer inputs to guide optimization, which also appears in layerwise natural-gradient methods [21, 22][21]T. Heskes. On "natural" learning and pruning in multilayered perceptrons. Neural Computation 12(4), 2000.[22]D. Povey et al. Parallel training of DNNs with natural gradient and parameter averaging, 2014.. Its matched-factor interpretation connects to work linking spectral-norm constraints with feature learning [23, 24][23]G. Yang et al. A spectral condition for feature learning, 2023.[24]J. Bernstein. Deriving Muon, 2025..

      Other methods construct their preconditioners from gradients. Shampoo and SOAP use gradient second-moment matrices [25, 26][25]V. Gupta et al. Mousse: Rectifying the geometry of Muon with curvature-aware preconditioning, 2026..

      A7Computational Cost

      MuonT adds about 1.5% to total training time in the 1.2B model comparison. The layer inputs are available before backpropagation, so we can compute the input statistics and preconditioning factors asynchronously while the backward pass runs. For the earlier (¼, ¼) implementation on H100s at a 2M-token batch, the measured step-time overhead is about 2% for the 130M–300M models and 3% for the 520M model. Storing the statistics and factors also requires additional memory.

      To reduce the cost of computing inverse powers, we reuse a recent eigenbasis and refine the factor for the current input statistic. If the refinement check fails, we take more iterations or recompute the factor by eigendecomposition.

      A8Supporting Experiments

      Here we describe how we measure and compare the effects discussed in Section 5. Most studies use earlier (¼, ¼) variants; the independent decay experiments use inner strength ½.

      Separating the inner and outer factors

      For the checkpoint experiment in Figure 6, we restart from the same nanoGPT checkpoint and replace selected Muon responses DviDv_iDvi​ with those from the inner-only (¼, 0) update. We change high-energy directions (λi≥tr⁡C/n\lambda_i\ge\tr C/nλi​≥trC/n), low-energy directions, or both. The subsequent data, learning rate and plain decay stay fixed, and wide matrices keep Muon’s update.

      Changed responsesFinal lossImprovement over Muon

      Table 1. Shared-checkpoint continuations at batch 2M. The Muon reference is one execution; the three modified updates average two executions with the same initialization and data, not independent seeds.

      Although these replacements approximately preserve response lengths, they can alter the angles between responses. Likewise, shuffling the weights or using a random input basis changes both which directions receive emphasis and how much the responses rotate.

      We examine outer scaling separately in runs trained from scratch. Keeping the inner strength at ½ and the learning rate fixed, we first introduce shaped decay, then add outer scaling with strength ¼. Comparing the runs before and after this final addition isolates the effect of outer scaling under the same decay rule.

      Curvature measurements

      High-energy input directions contribute more to feature changes. We also examine whether the loss is more sensitive to weight changes along those directions. For each input eigenvector viv_ivi​, we measure curvature along D=uvi⊤D=uv_i^{\top}D=uvi⊤​, averaging over random unit output directions uuu using exact Hessian–vector products.2020The directional curvature is ⟨D,HD⟩\langle D,HD\rangle⟨D,HD⟩, where HHH is the loss Hessian.

      The measured curvature is nearly proportional to input energy λi\lambda_iλi​, with median fitted exponents of 0.99 for the 77M model trained with Muon and 1.02 for nanoGPT trained with (¼, ¼) MuonT (Figure 13, curvature view). This agrees with the proportionality suggested by K-FAC’s factorization [6]. These measurements concern input eigendirections, not Hessian eigenvectors.

      This helps motivate smaller steps along high-energy directions. If directional curvature scales with λi\lambda_iλi​, an update whose length scales with λi−b\lambda_i^{-b}λi−b​ has a quadratic loss contribution proportional to

      λi(λi−b)2=λi1−2b.\lambda_i\big(\lambda_i^{-b}\big)^2=\lambda_i^{1-2b}.λi​(λi−b​)2=λi1−2b​.(6)

      Increasing the outer strength therefore reduces the relative contribution of high-energy directions. Whether the full update improves loss also depends on gradient alignment and interactions between parameter updates.

      Gradient noise

      The noise view of Figure 13 examines gradients along low-energy input directions, λi<tr⁡C/n\lambda_i<\tr C/nλi​<trC/n. We estimate how much of their squared magnitude comes from the mean gradient rather than sampling noise. For the gradient projected onto these directions, write S=∥Eg∥F2S=\|\E g\|_F^2S=∥Eg∥F2​ and assume noise energy ν/B\nu/Bν/B at batch BBB. The mean-gradient fraction is

      s(B)=SS+ν/B.s(B)=\frac{S}{S+\nu/B}.s(B)=S+ν/BS​.

      Assuming independent sampling, we estimate SSS from cross-products of gradient groups and scale microbatch noise estimates to the training batch. The mean-gradient fractions are 17–36% at batch 0.5M, 48–61% at 2M and 73% at 4M.

      In a separate experiment, we add noise equivalent to a 0.5M-token batch to selected input directions while training at batch 2M. Figure 13’s noise view shows how the loss advantage of (¼, ¼) MuonT over Muon changes depending on where we add the noise.

      Architecture and robustness checks

      We test whether the earlier (¼, ¼) recipe’s gains persist with GatedAttention [29][29]Z. Qiu et al. Gated attention for large language models: Non-linearity, sparsity, and attention-sink-free, 2025. and GatedNorm [30][30]Z. Qiu et al. A unified view of attention and residual sinks: Outlier-driven rescaling is essential for transformer training, 2026.. We also vary the root approximation, statistic averaging and damping to check sensitivity to these implementation choices (Figure 14).

      Toner retains about two thirds of its gain with GatedAttention and 88–95% with GatedNorm. GatedNorm raises both optimizers’ losses, especially Muon’s, so this comparison does not isolate the effect of removing outlier features.

      The largest loss increases in the robustness checks come from removing statistic averaging or increasing damping to 0.1.

      The dominant direction and the mean input

      To understand why one input direction carries so much energy, we examine the mean activation across tokens. Writing x=μ+ξx=\mu+\xix=μ+ξ, where μ=E[x]\mu=\E[x]μ=E[x], gives

      C=μμ⊤+E[ξξ⊤].C=\mu\mu^{\top}+\E[\xi\xi^{\top}].C=μμ⊤+E[ξξ⊤].

      This separates the contribution of the shared mean from variation around it. Efficient BackProp [31][31]Y. LeCun et al. Efficient BackProp. In Neural Networks: Tricks of the Trade, 1998. discusses how nonzero input means can worsen conditioning.

      At the Marin 130M model’s 4×-training checkpoint, the mean accounts for 96.3–98.4% of the energy along the dominant direction across attention layers 2 onward, measured by (v1⊤μ)2/λ1(v_1^{\top}\mu)^2/\lambda_1(v1⊤​μ)2/λ1​. Figure 15 shows layer 16, where this share is about 98.2%: ordinary tokens lie on the same side of zero along that direction. A weight update shifts their shared mean by ΔWμ\Delta W\muΔWμ.

      Update reversals

      We track how successive updates act along the dominant input direction by comparing Dtv1D_tv_1Dt​v1​ with Dt−1v1D_{t-1}v_1Dt−1​v1​. Across 72 hidden matrices at steps 101–400, these responses reverse in 88% of eligible pairs under Muon and 71% under (¼, ¼) MuonT. Figure 16 shows an example from one attention layer.2121We compare only steps with the same input basis, exclude decay from DtD_tDt​, and normalize response lengths by ∥Dt∥F/768\|D_t\|_F/\sqrt{768}∥Dt​∥F​/768​. The measurements use one nanoGPT run per optimizer at batch 2M; the Toner run uses (¼, ¼) with Frobenius rescaling.

      Fewer reversals do not necessarily mean faster convergence. For gradient descent on L(z)=12hz2L(z)=\tfrac12hz^2L(z)=21​hz2,

      zt+1=(1−ηh)zt,L(zt+1)L(zt)=(1−ηh)2.z_{t+1}=(1-\eta h)z_t,\qquad \frac{L(z_{t+1})}{L(z_t)}=(1-\eta h)^2.zt+1​=(1−ηh)zt​,L(zt​)L(zt+1​)​=(1−ηh)2.

      Both ηh=0.5\eta h=0.5ηh=0.5 and 1.51.51.5 reduce loss fourfold per step when zt≠0z_t\ne0zt​=0, although only the latter reverses direction. The reversal counts therefore describe a difference in training dynamics, rather than establish why Toner improves loss.2222Related oscillations occur at the edge of stability in full-batch gradient descent [32]. Applying this interpretation to Muon requires accounting for momentum and evolving optimizer state [33, 34]. Our fixed-statistic probes depend on momentum and do not establish an edge-of-stability explanation for these trajectories.
